q: What is the **synchronous speed** of a 4-pole motor on a 50 Hz supply?
What is the synchronous speed of an **8-pole** motor on 50 Hz?
w: 120 × 50 ÷ 8 = 750 rpm. More poles = slower speed.

q: A 4-pole, 50 Hz motor runs at **1420 rpm**. What is the slip?
What does **slip** mean in an induction motor?
o: The gap between rotor and stator
The difference between synchronous speed and rotor speed, as a % of synchronous speed
The loss of one phase while running
w: The rotor always runs a bit slower than the rotating field. That difference is the slip.

q: Why are motor rotors and cores **laminated**?
w: Thin insulated sheets break up the paths for eddy currents, so less heat and less loss.

q: Can a **shaded-pole** motor be reversed by swapping the supply leads?
o: Yes, swap the main winding leads
No — direction is set by where the shading rings are
w: The field always sweeps from the unshaded part of the pole to the shaded part. The rings are fixed, so the direction is fixed.

q: In a shaded-pole motor, what is the **shading ring** made of?
w: A thick copper ring around part of each pole. Induced current in it delays the flux in that part, creating a moving field.

q: On a **capacitor-start** motor, what disconnects the start winding?
w: At about 75 % of full speed the centrifugal switch opens and the start winding drops out.

q: How do you **reverse** a series universal motor?
o: Reverse the connections to the field OR the armature (not both)
w: Reversing only one of them changes the direction. Reversing both leaves it the same.

q: Maximum torque in a 3-phase induction motor happens when rotor resistance equals…
w: Max torque when R₂ = X₂. A rotor-resistance (slip-ring) starter adds resistance at start to get max torque at standstill.

q: With a **star-delta** starter, the starting current is about…
w: In star each winding gets 230 V instead of 400 V, so starting current and torque drop to about one third.

q: What is **single phasing**?
o: Running a motor on a single-phase supply
Loss of one phase while a 3-phase motor is running
Using one overload for three phases
w: The motor keeps turning but draws too much current in the other two windings, so it overheats and can burn out.

q: **No-volt protection** on a motor starter is there to…
o: Stop the motor restarting by itself when power comes back
w: If the supply drops, the contactor drops out. The hold-in (retaining) contact is lost, so someone has to press Start again.

q: A series R-L-C circuit is at **resonance**. Which is true?
o: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, so Z = R and current is at its maximum
w: The two reactances cancel, leaving only R. Lowest impedance → biggest current, power factor 1.

q: Which formula gives the **resonant frequency**?
w: f₀ = 1 ÷ (2π √(L × C)). Remember to convert µF to F first.

q: In a mainly **inductive** circuit the current…
o: is in phase with the voltage
w: Inductive = lagging. Capacitive = leading. Memory trick: CIVIL — in a C, I before V; V before I in an L.

q: Power factor equals…
w: pf = cos φ = R ÷ Z = True power ÷ Apparent power (P ÷ S).

q: In a parallel R-L-C circuit, I<sub>R</sub> = 9 A, I<sub>L</sub> = 15 A, I<sub>C</sub> = 3 A. The circuit is…
w: I<sub>L</sub> is bigger than I<sub>C</sub>, so the circuit is inductive overall → lagging.

q: What does X<sub>C</sub> do when frequency goes **up**?
w: X<sub>C</sub> = 1 ÷ (2πfC). Higher f → smaller X<sub>C</sub>. X<sub>L</sub> does the opposite.

q: In a **delta** connection, line current equals…
w: Delta: V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>, I<sub>L</sub> = √3 × I<sub>ph</sub>.

q: In a **star** connection on a 400 V supply, the phase voltage is…
w: Star: V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> ÷ √3 = 400 ÷ 1.732 = 230.940 V. I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>.

q: Total power of a balanced 3-phase load is…
w: P = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ. Or 3 × V<sub>ph</sub> × I<sub>ph</sub> × cos φ — same answer.

q: How do you find total power with the **two-wattmeter** method?
w: On a 3-phase 3-wire system, total power = the sum of the two readings.

q: Flux density B equals…
w: B = Φ ÷ A, in tesla (T). Convert cm² to m² by dividing by 10,000.

q: A **low-loss** magnetic material has a hysteresis loop that is…
w: Narrow loop = little energy lost each cycle → good for transformer cores. Wide loop = high loss → good for permanent magnets.

q: The **time constant** of an R-C circuit is…
w: τ = R × C (in seconds). Fully charged after about 5 time constants.

q: 68 µF in series with 47 kΩ. Time constant?
Initial charging current of a capacitor = …
w: At switch-on the capacitor acts like a short, so I₀ = V ÷ R.

q: How many diodes in a **three-phase full-wave** bridge rectifier?
w: Two diodes per phase × 3 phases = 6.

q: Compared with single-phase, a 3-phase rectifier has…
w: The peaks overlap, so the DC is much smoother (less ripple).

q: A **photodiode** normally works in…
w: Reverse biased: light frees charge carriers and a small reverse current flows in proportion to the light.

q: In an NPN transistor, which current is the **largest**?
w: I<sub>E</sub> = I<sub>B</sub> + I<sub>C</sub>, so the emitter current is the biggest.

q: What causes the **depletion layer** in a P-N junction?
o: Electrons and holes crossing the junction and recombining
w: Near the junction, free electrons fill holes. That leaves a thin zone with no free carriers, which acts as a barrier.

q: An LED runs from 48 V. It needs 2 V at 20 mA. What series resistor?
One disadvantage of a **linear** power supply is…
o: heavy and wastes energy as heat
w: Advantage: simple, clean output, low noise. Disadvantage: big transformer, heavy, inefficient.

q: On an oscilloscope showing AC, the **X-axis** shows…
w: X (horizontal) = time (time/div). Y (vertical) = voltage (volts/div). The Y-plates move the beam up and down.

q: A signal is **21.21 V RMS**. What is its peak voltage?
Colour code for 3-phase cores: L1, L2, L3 are…
w: L1 brown, L2 black, L3 grey. Blue = neutral only. Green/yellow = protective conductor only.

q: AC cables entering a **ferromagnetic** (steel) enclosure must be arranged so…
o: each conductor has its own steel entry hole
all conductors of the circuit, including the CPC, go through together
only the line goes through steel
w: Conductors must only be surrounded by steel together, never one by one — otherwise eddy currents heat the steel.

q: PVC/PVC cable will touch **expanded polystyrene** in a cavity. What do you do?
o: Put it in conduit or another barrier so it does not touch
w: Polystyrene draws the plasticiser out of PVC and the insulation goes brittle. Keep them apart.

q: Unprotected cable buried in a wall is allowed within **150 mm** of…
w: Safe zones: within 150 mm of the ceiling, within 150 mm of a corner, or straight vertical/horizontal runs to an accessory. Check the exact wording in ET101.

q: In a hollow wall, the cable must be at least ___ from the **reverse side** of the wall.
w: Not less than 50 mm from the back face, so a screw from the other side will not hit it. Check in ET101.

q: An aluminium conductor is about ___ as conductive as copper.
w: About 61 %, so aluminium needs a bigger size (usually one size up) for the same current. It is lighter and cheaper.

q: Joining aluminium to copper, you should use…
o: a bi-metallic lug, clean and dry, with contact grease
w: Stops electrolytic corrosion. Keep it dry, clean, isolated, and torque it correctly.

q: One advantage of **XLPE** over PVC insulation is…
o: higher operating temperature, so more current for the same size
it does not need a sheath
w: XLPE runs at 90 °C vs 70 °C for PVC, so it carries more current. It also lasts longer and handles overloads better.

q: Low-voltage and **ELV** cables in the same trunking are OK if…
o: every cable is insulated for the highest voltage present
w: Or: separate compartments, a partition on tray, or separate conduit/trunking (ET101 528.1).

q: Maximum length of the **permanent link** (patch panel to outlet) for Cat5e/Cat6?
w: 90 m permanent link + up to 10 m of patch/work-area leads = 100 m channel.

q: What makes an **STP** cable different from UTP?
o: It has a foil/metal shield around the pairs
w: Both have 4 twisted pairs with different twist rates and an outer jacket. STP adds a shield against interference (EMI).

q: **Discrimination** between protective devices means…
o: the device nearest the fault (supply side) operates first
the main fuse always goes first
w: Only the fuse/MCB just upstream of the fault should go, so the rest of the installation stays on.

q: HBC stands for…
w: HBC fuses can safely break very high fault currents, and discriminate well, so they back up MCBs.

q: On an RCD marked **32A / 30mA / AC**, what is 30 mA?
o: The residual (leakage) current that will trip it
w: 32 A = how much load it can carry. 30 mA = sensitivity. AC = type (for loads with no significant DC component).

q: An MCB has two trip actions. Overloads are handled by the…
w: Thermal = slow, for overloads. Magnetic = instant, for short circuits.

q: In a **fuse-switch**…
o: the fuse is a separate box next to the switch
the fuse link forms the moving contact
the switch is inside the fuse
w: Fuse-switch: the fuse carrier moves as the switch blade. Switch-fuse: a switch with fuses in series in one unit.

q: Thermistors for motor protection are fitted…
w: Embedded in the windings and wired to a thermistor relay that opens the control circuit if they heat up.

q: A thermostat's **bi-metallic strip** works because…
o: two metals expand by different amounts, so the strip bends
w: The bend opens or closes the contacts.

q: Where is a distribution board **NOT** allowed?
w: Also not in bathrooms/WCs, storage or airing cupboards, above cookers/heaters, or where clothes could cover it (ET101 530.5).

q: A new bearing is pressed onto a shaft. The press should push on…
w: Pressing the outer race forces load through the balls and damages them. Remove old bearings with a puller.

q: Alignment of a direct coupling is finally checked with…
o: a feeler gauge at 4 points 90° apart
w: Straight edge first, then feeler gauge at four points. All four the same = aligned.

q: A **flexible coupling** is used because it…
o: absorbs shock, vibration and small misalignment
w: It also allows for shaft expansion.

q: Why is there a cheaper **Night Saver** rate?
o: Demand is lowest overnight, so power stations sit idle
w: Peak is around 17:00–19:00. The valley is overnight. Cheap rates fill the valley and use plant better.

q: Difference between **SELV** and **PELV**?
o: SELV is separated from earth; PELV can be earthed
w: Both are extra-low voltage. SELV is fully separated from earth; PELV is not.

q: 10 cells of 1.5 V, each 0.2 Ω internal, feed a 4 Ω load. Current?
When testing lead-acid batteries, why is **ventilation** needed?
o: Charging gives off hydrogen, which can explode
w: No naked flames. Wear goggles, rubber gloves and an apron.

q: In a **maintained** emergency light the lamp…
o: is on all the time, mains or battery
w: Non-maintained: only on during mains failure. Combined (sustained): has two or more lamps, one fed from the emergency supply.

q: Quarterly test on a **3-hour** self-contained fitting: simulate mains failure for at least…
w: At least 30 min (10 min for 1-hour units), but not more than a quarter of rated duration. Annual test = full rated duration.

q: The unit of **illuminance** is…
w: Luminous flux = lumens. Illuminance = lux = lumens falling on each square metre.

q: Low-pressure sodium (SOX) lamps are known for…
o: very high efficiency but poor colour (yellow light)
w: Monochromatic yellow light, so colours look wrong. Used where colour does not matter, like roads.

q: Night storage heaters store heat in…
w: They charge on off-peak electricity. The damper controls how fast heat is released.

q: **Main protective bonding** connects…
o: extraneous-conductive parts (water, gas pipes) to the main earthing terminal
w: It keeps all metalwork at the same potential, so dangerous touch voltages cannot build up during a fault.

q: Why fit **expansion joints** on long busbar runs?
o: To let the bars expand and contract with heat
w: Without them the bars can warp, clearances shrink, and joints loosen into high-resistance hot spots.

q: In an **IP** rating, the second digit is protection against…
w: First digit = solids/dust. Second digit = water. E.g. IP55.

q: External influence codes starting with **A** describe…
w: A = environment, B = utilisation (people), C = construction of the building. AD = water, AE = solid objects/dust.

q: Which MCB type is for **very high** inrush current (transformers, welders)?
w: B trips at 3–5 × In, C at 5–10 × In, D at 10–20 × In. Bigger inrush → later letter.

q: A Type **C** MCB trips instantly (magnetic) at about…
w: Type C suits inductive loads like fluorescent lighting and small motors.

q: Faults at A (near the supply), B and C (far end). Fault current is **lowest** at…
w: The further from the transformer, the more impedance in the loop, so the less fault current.

q: Why must T-568A and T-568B **not** be mixed in one installation?
o: The green and orange pairs swap pins, so data will not pass
w: Pick one standard and stick to it. Mixed ends are only for crossover leads.

q: Minimum clearance between underground **communication** cables and **power** cables?
w: 100 mm, or use a fire-retardant partition, or mechanical protection at crossings (ET101 528.2).

q: Cable buried between two buildings must be…
o: marked with cable covers or warning tape
w: Plus protection against damage (or buried deep enough), and buried ducts identified.

q: Recommended minimum bending radius of an **aluminium-sheathed** cable?
w: r = 15 × D, where D is the outside diameter of the cable.

q: A "Solar PV on roof" sign is **not** required at…
w: Signs go at the origin, the meter (if remote), and the board the inverter connects to.

q: What does **DCL** stand for when connecting a luminaire?
w: Luminaires connect via a box, a DCL outlet, or equipment designed for direct connection.

q: Supplementary bonding conductor where it is **not** mechanically protected — minimum size?
w: 4 mm² unprotected, 2.5 mm² where mechanically protected (ET101 544.2).

q: A DB with its bottom **below 1.4 m** must be…
w: So young children cannot get at it (ET101 530.6).

q: Steel conduit is used as the CPC. How many cables do you count per single-phase circuit?
w: The conduit itself is the protective conductor, so only line and neutral are drawn in.

q: Cable factor for a stranded **2.5 mm²** PVC single-core in conduit (long runs/bends)?
w: From the papers' model answers: 1.5 mm² = 22, 2.5 mm² = 30 (Table 52J.3). Check against ET101.

q: A hydrometer measures the…
w: Fully charged lead-acid reads about 1.25–1.28.

q: VRLA (sealed lead-acid) batteries are charged by…
w: Constant voltage for lead-acid. Ni-Cad uses constant current.

q: Compared with lead-acid, Ni-Cad batteries are…
o: lighter, dearer, and last much longer
w: About 50–60 % lighter, higher initial cost, 25+ years life.

q: **Annual** test of a 3-hour self-contained emergency light: run on battery for…
w: Quarterly: 30 min. Annual: full rated duration. Record everything in the logbook.

q: One advantage of a **self-contained** system over a central battery system:
o: a failure only affects one fitting
w: Self-contained: cheap to install, independent. Central: long battery life, central testing, but one failure kills all.

q: Approximate efficacy of **LED** lamps?
w: Fluorescent about 30–70 lm/W. LED about 100–200 lm/W. Both full output at switch-on.

q: Which lamp has the **highest efficacy** but the **worst** colour rendering?
w: SOX about 180 lm/W, monochrome yellow light. MBF about 50 lm/W, reasonable colour.

q: An instrument that measures lighting level in a room is a…
w: It reads illuminance (E) in lux.

q: Room 8 m × 16 m needs 300 lux. Total luminous flux?
In N = F ÷ (n × lm × UF × MF), what is **MF**?
o: Maintenance factor — allows for dirt and lamp ageing
w: UF = utilisation factor (how much light reaches the work plane). MF = maintenance factor.

q: Best control for lights next to big office windows?
w: Also PIR presence detection, dimmable fittings, and a central lighting control system.

q: On a fan-assisted storage heater, the **fan** is fed from the…
w: Elements charge on off-peak (restricted). The fan must work during the day, so unrestricted.

q: Why must storage heaters be fixed securely?
o: The heat-storage blocks make them very heavy
w: High-density clay/ceramic blocks: strong wall fixing and a floor that can take the weight.

q: How does the supply authority control off-peak storage heating?
o: With a sealed time switch on a separate circuit and an off-peak meter
w: Separate circuit, sealed time switch, separate meter.

q: Underfloor heating mat under tiles. Which is **wrong**?
o: Cut the mat shorter to fit
w: Never cut or overlap heating cable — the mat is designed for a set wattage.

q: An **S-Plan** system uses…
o: a 2-port zone valve for each zone
w: S-Plan: 2-port valve per zone. Y-Plan: one 3-port mid-position valve.

q: A **Y-Plan** system uses…
w: The mid-position valve can feed heating, hot water, or both at once.

q: Equipment marked with the **double-square** symbol should…
o: be bonded to the gas pipe
w: Double-square = double insulated (Class II). No earth connection.

q: Which of these is **not** one of the standard verification tests?
w: Visual inspection, continuity of protective conductors, insulation resistance, polarity, earth fault loop impedance, RCD operation.

q: Two types of flange misalignment are…
w: Angular: gap wider one side. Parallel: shaft centres offset. Correct both to the maker's tolerance.

q: Which is an **advantage** of rising main busbar over cables?
o: Less termination space and can be reused
w: Also: fewer fixings, faster install, type-tested fault rating, better fire resistance, lower volt drop.
